studentOpening: hey, so module 3 tomorrow and i'm kinda lost on dp. i can memorize the definitions but like... i don't actually *get* why greedy works sometimes and not others? and everyone keeps talking about overlapping subproblems but i have no idea what that looks like lol. can we go through this properly?
tutorTurns: Picture picking movies tonight so none of the showtimes overlap — that's activity selection, greedy's bread and butter, and it just works there. In your own words, what do you think "greedy" is actually doing when it picks an option — and why's your gut say that breaks for something like knapsack?

That's exactly right — end-time first, correct move choice, and you nailed why knapsack breaks it: greedy commits to each pick without seeing how it forecloses better combinations later. Here's the sharper version: in knapsack, could swapping in that one heavy item ever require *un-picking* something greedy already locked in?

Yes — exactly. Greedy makes one irreversible pass; DP explores the branches greedy would've skipped and picks the winner. Now here's where it gets expensive: exploring "what if I skip this item" and "what if I skip that other item" often leads you back to asking the exact same sub-question — like "best value using items 1-3 with 7kg left" — from multiple different paths. Why would recomputing that same answer twice be a problem?

Exactly — memoization is caching each subproblem's answer the first time so repeat visits are instant. Matrix chain multiplication also has overlapping subproblems, but there's no items to grab or skip — you're deciding where to place parentheses when multiplying a chain of matrices. What do you think the "subproblem" even is there?

That subproblem definition — cheapest cost to multiply matrices i through j — is exactly right, that's the real formulation. The confusion is legit too: knapsack subproblems are one-dimensional (which items so far), but here you're tracking a whole range (i,j) AND trying every possible split point inside it. Is it the range-tracking that's fuzzy, or picking which split point is best?

You basically built the whole DP intuition tonight yourself — why greedy locks in choices, why that's fine for activity selection but wrecks knapsack, what overlapping subproblems actually looks like, and even the right subproblem definition for matrix chain. The one place you genuinely stalled was visualizing two-index ranges instead of counting items one by one — that's real, not a knowledge gap. Bring these tomorrow:

1. "Is there a trick for holding (i,j) ranges in your head, or does everyone trip on that jump at first?"
2. "How do you tell upfront whether a new problem needs 2D range subproblems like matrix chain, or 1D ones like knapsack?"
